analysis.investment_thesis: Jindal Saw is a capital-intensive iron and steel pipe manufacturer riding India's infrastructure and water-sector tailwinds, with recently improved profitability — ROCE has reached 19.4% and operating income nearly doubled over 2023-2025. However, the cyclical, commodity-like nature of the business, high absolute finance costs (INR 623 Cr versus net profit of INR 1,458 Cr), and dependence on government capex cycles make this a fair business rather than a wonderful one.
key_strengths: ROE of 16.3% and ROCE of 19.4% cross my 15% threshold — driven by genuine operating leverage with EBITDA CAGR of 14% over 9 years
Operating cash flow positive all 5 years (2020-2025), generating INR 2,335 Cr OCF in FY25 — the business actually produces cash
Reasonable valuation at 13.4x P/E and 0.82x P/S with a manageable D/E of 0.44, leaving some margin of safety
key_risks: Capital-intensive steel pipe business with limited pricing power — commodity inputs (steel) compress margins during downturns as seen in FY2021-22
Finance costs of INR 623 Cr annually consume roughly 43% of net profit, leaving the equity holder with thin protection in a downturn
Net profit was negative in 2016 and 2018, confirming the cyclicality that I deeply dislike — I cannot predict earnings with confidence 10 years out
red_flags: No durable competitive moat — pipes are largely commoditized and contracts are won on price
Revenue essentially flat in FY2025 (INR 20,829 Cr) versus FY2024 (INR 20,958 Cr) despite strong infrastructure spending — growth may be plateauing
High dependence on government infrastructure orders introduces regulatory and payment-cycle risk
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Jindal Saw has clearly improved its financial profile over the last three years — EBITDA jumped from INR 1,674 Cr in FY2023 to INR 3,423 Cr in FY2025, and the balance sheet has strengthened with equity growing from INR 7,921 Cr to INR 12,083 Cr. At 13.4x earnings and 8x EV/EBITDA for a business with real assets and consistent cash flows, the valuation is fair but not compellingly cheap.

My objection is structural, not numerical: I cannot identify what prevents a competitor from taking business away from Jindal Saw at the next contract tender. Steel pipes are not See's Candies. When I buy a business, I want to be certain it will earn good returns on capital for 20 years regardless of who manages it. The earnings history — losses in 2016 and 2018, near-zero growth periods — tells me this business requires skilled navigation of commodity cycles. That is work I do not wish to depend on.
